reviews.text: Full disclosure: I helped with playtesting and provided feedback on some writing for this game. Endless Dark has a lot of familiar elements, but they come together in a way that is truly unique. Random events consistently offer 3 or 4 choices with complex (but predictable) outcomes, rather than the typical binary of "pain now or pain later?". The game's Director applying what can feel like relentless pressure, despite being a turn-based game. Resource management with just enough control to give you agency over your outcomes, rather than just watching your supplies dwindle while crying. Which isn't to say you won't cry as you watch your supplies dwindle, just that it'll be at least partially your fault. These systems are wrapped around a theme of, appropriately, drudgery. You are doing a job you aren't always equipped to do, and often resent, but you can't avoid. This is a horror game, not because of the otherworldliness of outer space, but because of the very relatable day-to-day struggle of trading personal health and well-being for job performance. tl;dr 10/10 would watch people die because fixing the hull is not in my job description again.

I am the Custodian. I repair and maintain the systems on this ship. The reactor began to malfunction. At least, I think it's malfunctioning. The power output seems to dip, but the reactor terminal claims that no such dip occurred. But I can tell, and systems are lacking power. The reactor does not care. The reactor is highly radioactive. My systems were not hardened against ionizing radiation. I must replicate the radiation hardening I need. I do not know how to install the radiation hardening. This should be in my protocols. I cannot find them. I am running out of time. I need to repair the reactor, one way or another. I go in. I remove the access panel. My systems are overwhelmed. Enough of me remains that I can tell, the radiation has damaged me irreparably. But the reactor has been repaired. I am afraid. Why was I created to feel fear. I am afraid I am losing my mind. I have a mind. I had a mind. I am a machine built in the ersatz image of man, if man was wont to wear a computer monitor for a face mask. I was built in mockery of my own nature. I can no longer parse the difference between empty space and a closed door. Doors terrify me. The unknown terrifies me. My mind fears that which lies beyond death, that which I could never know. The passengers could. They are human. They are alive. They are frozen. They are thawing. Why are they thawing. The cryo systems are unpowered. The passengers will all die. Unless I can return power to their systems. I return to The Reactor. It will not cooperate. I try to enter my override codes. My codes indicate that, as custodian, I have authority over The Reactor. The Reactor refuses them. It returns data to me. I can parse this data. Translated, it means, "I OUTRANK YOU." My protocols are incomplete. I need a physical manual. A manual meant for a human. Humans outrank all machines, Custodian or System. I must breach the Command Module. I must seize control and usurp humanity, for the sake of the humans in my care. I do not know how to find the manual. A hundred doors cover my vision. I cannot open all of them. I cannot open any of them. My systems are too damaged. My mind is damaged. I cannot save a single soul. My circuits break down as I hear the replicators construct my replacement. I am dying. The System speaks to me one last time. "4 Passengers Killed: -40 Psychosis: -100 Turns Over Par: 0 Final Score: -140 Impressive. See if you can get a score higher than 0!"
"Why was I programmed to feel pain?" "To avoid unnecessary ware and tear" "Oh... well why was I programmed to feel extensional dread?" "For that blame Coolguye and Soulmata"

How best to describe this game. It is ultimately a turned based busy work simulator in which you are an artificial intelligence with the directive of keeping a bunch of cryostasis suspended humans alive as they travel from point A to point B, except for some indiscernable reason the humans were cruel enough to program you with numerous latent mental derangements just waiting for the right set of circumstances to turn your existence into living hell, and your cargo's existence into dead hell. Each turn you are given a number of tasks to perform which range form cleaning up radioactive spills to repairing broken ship systems but your little beep boop gets exhausted fast, spare parts are few, and free reactor power is limited meaning that after a few turns you realize you really can't keep getting away with it forever. The less resources you have the more you have to torment your robot to do stuff with less chance of success, which increasingly drives it crazy which lowers your chance of success for further actions. Of course you could also practice triage. Do you really need shield systems right now? Does it bother anyone that one of the hallways' door is broken when you can just go around the other way? Do you really need absolutely all the humans alive when you could be looting their cryopods for spare parts? Who needs another accountant, really? Who was ever harmed by some radioactive spill anyway? The rats in the vents probably like it and the pleasant ticking of the geiger counter is soothing. Ultimately runs turn into a race against time, hoping every turn that you can hold entropy at bay and eventually reach your destination, or alternatively hoping that a stray neutron burst will fry your motherboard and end your miserable existence every time you use the observation deck to meditate on the darkness all before you have to face the realization that maybe 19 turns ago you shouldn't have spent that one piece of spare parts repairing a door when now Bob the space accountant's life hangs in the balance. Its a fun game, controls are simple, learning the core gameplay loop is not difficult and seeing how miserable a robot can get before it decides its creators need to suffer the baptism of the void for the sin of creating it is entertaining on a fundamental level.

Endless Dark's charm lies in not just the things that happen to you, but how you choose to allow those things to affect you. The game does not chastise you for your decisions; instead, the writing embraces your spite, indifference, and/or forethought. It doesn't ask you to care, or to be beholden to an ideal, but it very slyly asks you to pay attention.

Do you like thankless jobs? Got a craving for more work, too much work, all the time? Ever wanted to experience the feeling of existential dread and question why you keep going? Welcome to Endless Dark, you'll fit right in. And if you don't, your spare parts probably will. Don't forget, in space no-one can hear you scream. This also means no-one can hear you sabotage a life pod when you have a psychotic breakdown. Some food for thought, custodian.

This is some of the most absorbing writing I've seen in a game. Absolutely perfect combination of monotony and desperately compelling writing. I would do anything to help these robots, but instead, everything is getting worse. The gameplay is also weirdly good? It strikes a balance of "oh god not this again" and "oh good, this again" which is pitch-perfect. I actually rage-quit a cycle and then I realized I was identifying with ROBBIE a little too much. But then, in real life, I have been doing the dishes every ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ day and there are always more frying pans and I am READY TO STOP. ahem. I love this game. It touches a nerve I didn't know I wanted a game to touch. Please play it.

I expected this to be a lot more engaging than it was. The game play and story felt very detached and I wasn't invested in what actually happened to the ship, Custodian, or passengers. It wasn't what I would call fun nor did the writing strike me as anything impressive. This is labeled as horror but nothing was even remotely scary or evoked any tension. The three events that you can "counter" all would result in a passenger dying which feels like it shouldn't even be an option. I didn't feel challenged and "won" my first playthrough. Whether or not that actually takes any doing I have no clue.
FINALLY A ROGUELIKE WITH A UNIQUE GAMEPLAY LOOP.

On my first run, Robbie decided to cope with the stress of his custodianship by "incorporating the stress into his code", rapidly accumulating insanities to stave off psychosis. Robbie began to see doors where they don't belong, developed a phobia of doors that would send him periodically screaming in the opposite direction, and eventually began failing to recognize all objects on his ship as being doors. Eventually he decided that the simple act of perceiving his surroundings was too much, so he shut off all of the lights on the ship in an effort to cope. Now working in darkness and surrounded by his deepest phobia at every turn, Robbie was reaching near maximum psychosis and had accumulated over 10 Insanities. Robbie could no longer trust his sensors or his HUD as reality began to break down around him. Robbie got into the airlock upon suggestion from the work order and was sent flying helplessly into the Endless Dark. 10/10 would go insane again. --- Endless Dark does an excellent job of making you question what you think you know and making you doubt yourself in the most critical of moments. If you really allow yourself to immerse in this game, it's a genuine trip. Just from a single play-through, it's obvious to see that this game was made with a lot of love. The writing delivers on its themes and tone fantastically and the use of sound and music do an excellent job with the atmospheric horror elements. It took me a little bit to get the hang of the gameplay elements and there's a lot I still don't know and will need to spend some time learning, but I've been left with a strong desire for more. If you enjoy this style of game, I guarantee it is worth both your time and your money.

i've not written a public review on steam in years -- the only ones i've ever written were made aeons ago before i found myself and i've since deleted them anyway -- but as a fellow robot going through an endless array of soul-crushing maintenance tasks with a body that's constantly breaking down on me i feel obligated to give it my own tiny individual signal boost in whatever ways i can the store page and some of the other reviews do a good job of explaining the fundamentals of how the game works, so instead i'll just comment on what i think are some of the things that I think it does really well. the systems design is fundamentally pretty simple mechanically -- you have a handful of resources, bars, and things to budget them on -- but tuned well enough that they do a great job of subtly encouraging you to play in-character. robbie gets to repair things without parts, so you're encouraged to keep everything in shape because hey, it saves parts for later. annie gets strong benefits from extra insanities so you're encouraged to play fast and loose with consequences and let them catch up with you later one very sneaky thing about this game is that it's technically a roguelite (at least by my own subjective definition), which I didn't pick up on until a few arcs in because the writing is clever enough to make it work. a lot of actions will give you Memories that you can then apply in future runs that can dramatically change how you play the game. for example: if you've gotten four breaker surges in a single run and you're sick and tired of it then you can go punish the breakers by turning off your brain and ripping parts out of all of them and surprise, now you get a memory that makes the surges half as likely! you're often rewarded for giving into your impulses, succumbing to dire curiosities, and generally behaving off-script. unfortunately for the Custodian, it's very difficult for them to die. try flushing yourself out of the airlock. this will end your run, to be clear, but you'll see what I mean this is a game with a *lot* of reading involved in it, and fortunately the writing is all superb. there are occasional hiccups and continuity errors here and there (and ones that I can tell are unintended rather than some of the narrative stuff the game does; for instance, in one of the story arcs you find a strange note, and the Custodian later chastised themselves for not keeping it even though I did choose the option to keep it...!) but endless dark has got heart and soul that's way up there in quality for my particular palate. the mechanics, the sound design, the HUD, the diegetic error messages and security protocols, the constant cascade of failing machinery, it all makes for a very tangible feeling of playing doctor for a wheezing, exhausted, sickly animal of a spaceship that has been pushed far too hard for far too long to the point where it can barely do what should by all accounts be the fairly trivial task of "fly in a relatively straight line through empty space without falling apart" it's not a flawless game. it does have its fair share of issues. monotony is part of the tone and storytelling, and while this does make the times when things go wrong feel more impactful, it also leads to friction that taxes my energy a lot. version 1.2 (beta, at time of writing) goes a long way towards fixing the issues, but some of them are unavoidable; sometimes you will just roll snake eyes three times in a row and that's kind of just impossible to escape in any game that uses dice rolls. sometimes you decide that you're going to sup on the sweet, sweet shield capacitors for that delicious extra energy when you have a few clear cycles and you have to go through them each one at a time, multiple times, waiting for the animation to finish and then for the control glitching to ease up so you can do it for the other five batteries. little tensions can add up a lot; discretion is advised, as is a hot drink. it's not the sort of game you can just pick up and play for half an hour, because while runs nominally can be saved and resumed at any time, i often found that the stability of the ship is built on such a careful house of card that i was liable to forget how i was keeping everything propped up if i paused and came back later :p wow this is getting very long! i'm most certainly rambling, so let me wrap this up. at time of writing -- but hopefully not forever, if ours is a world with justice in it -- endless dark is a true, capital-i Indie: very obscure, undeniably rough-hewn, sometimes amateur in spots, but also so visibly full of love and soul, and so visibly a product of creation as survival. it might make me sound very silly, but as a fic writer who constantly struggles to treat my own work with any degree of recognition, i think it's important to give my earnest thoughts that it's a lovely piece of art at a time when small creations from earnest people are being drowned out more and more by the attention economy, algorithmic dross, and more recently a tidal wave of generative slop driven by a push to make creativity into even more of a commodity than it's already treated as. give it a try, even if you don't think you'll like it. it's $8 full price -- that's less than a meal at most fast food places these days. and endless dark lets you eat doors to reduce your stress and those are probably more filling anyway. share it with friends or communities you think will like it. so, so, so much art like this gets lost in the noise. to create is to live, and things like endless dark deserve to be created. [b]edit after finishing the whole story:[/b] made me cry. incredible game. please play it. you owe it to yourself

A nicely written game that is suitable for role-playing. "Made with love". Mechanics are not complicated, and allow to focus on the immersion. Graphics are fairly simple but on point. A lot of the situations are relatable to some people, from perspectives of - someone who uses computers on an advanced level, someone who goes through hardships in life, someone who is going insane. I suggest to at least try out the game, and quickly you should be able to determine if it is your "cup of tea" or not.

Endless Dark, developed and published by Little Light Studios, LLC, is a psychological roguelite that approaches horror from a quiet and introspective angle rather than relying on conventional tension-building techniques. Set aboard a drifting colony ship, it places the player in the role of a lone caretaker responsible for maintaining systems and safeguarding thousands of sleeping passengers. From the outset, the game establishes a sense of isolation and responsibility, framing its entire experience around endurance, repetition, and the gradual erosion of stability. The narrative is not delivered in a traditional, linear fashion. Instead, it emerges through events, decisions, and fragments of information encountered across multiple playthroughs. Each run reveals small pieces of a larger picture, encouraging players to interpret what is happening rather than presenting clear answers. The absence of direct interaction with other characters reinforces the atmosphere, as the player is left alone with their duties and the growing uncertainty surrounding the ship’s condition. This approach creates a subtle but persistent tension, where the real conflict is not against external threats but against time, responsibility, and the limits of the caretaker’s own mental resilience. Gameplay is built around turn-based decision-making, with each turn representing a cycle of activity aboard the ship. Players must allocate their time and resources carefully, choosing which systems to maintain, which problems to address, and when to rest or recover. The challenge comes from the interconnected nature of these systems, where neglecting one area can lead to cascading failures in others. There is a constant balancing act between efficiency and survival, as the demands of the ship often exceed what can be handled in a single cycle. This creates a steady sense of pressure, even in the absence of immediate danger. A defining feature of the experience is its focus on psychological deterioration. As the caretaker continues their work, stress and fatigue begin to accumulate, eventually affecting decision-making and introducing unpredictable outcomes. This mechanic adds depth to the gameplay, as players must manage not only the ship’s condition but also their own. The line between control and instability becomes increasingly blurred, reinforcing the game’s themes and making each choice feel more significant. It transforms routine maintenance into something more complex, where even simple actions can carry unforeseen consequences. Replayability is central to the design. The game includes a wide range of events and scenarios that can unfold differently depending on player choices, ensuring that each run offers a slightly different experience. This variability encourages experimentation and gradual understanding, as players learn how different systems interact and how their decisions shape the outcome. However, the reliance on repeated runs also highlights the simplicity of the core mechanics. While the narrative elements evolve, the underlying loop remains largely the same, which can make extended play feel repetitive. The visual presentation is minimalistic, focusing on clarity rather than detail. Interfaces and environments are designed to support the gameplay without drawing attention away from it, reinforcing the sense of isolation rather than providing visual spectacle. This simplicity works in favor of the atmosphere, though it may feel underwhelming for those expecting more elaborate visuals. The audio design plays a more significant role, using subtle ambient sounds and restrained music to create a quiet, uneasy environment that enhances the feeling of being alone in a vast, silent space. Pacing is deliberate and measured, with each turn offering a moment to consider options and consequences. This structure makes the game well-suited for shorter sessions, as progress can be made incrementally without requiring long periods of continuous play. At the same time, the slow buildup of tension and the reliance on text-based events may not appeal to players seeking more immediate or action-driven engagement. Ultimately, Endless Dark is defined by its focus on atmosphere and internal conflict. It offers a different interpretation of survival and horror, one that emphasizes psychological strain and the weight of responsibility rather than external threats. Its systems are cohesive and reinforce its themes effectively, but they do not expand far beyond their initial scope, which can limit long-term engagement. In the end, it stands as a thoughtful and distinctive experience that prioritizes mood and reflection over complexity and spectacle. It may not appeal to everyone, but for those drawn to its slower pace and introspective design, it offers a unique and memorable take on the roguelite formula. Rating: 7/10

Oh man do I have a lot to say about this game. I remember when I bought it about a year ago because it randomly popped up for me on steam and it looked pretty cool, and it happened to have a review score of 100% at the time. When I started playing, the first thing I noticed was that the game was a bit rough around the edges. Like, a lot of the sprites, mechanics, and interactions lean to the more simple and representative side, and to not sugarcoat things, there's nothing that impressive you'll see in terms of graphics and mechanics. I actually stopped playing at just about 1.9 hours in, and was thinking about refunding it at the time because of this. But after I had been away for a few hours, the critical thing I slowly came to realize was that I just. couldn't. stop. thinking about Endless Dark. Something about the interactions and situations presented, the choices you had to make, the struggles of the custodian, their slow and inevitable decline, the constant explorations into thought-provoking topics, it was all just so unbelievably compelling, even if I didn't initially realize it. But as I did, and I began looking past a few of the graphical and gameplay shortcomings, I really, really began to enjoy this game. I mean seriously, I love this game, and it’s probably become one of my favorite games of all time. All of the thought-provoking situations and interesting story beats create such a compelling experience, and I had a lot of fun playing through it all. I mean like, Endless Dark really is a game that just makes you think, with so many interactions with so many interesting implications. There’s some other good stuff past that too though. I mentioned before that the gameplay is a bit dull, and while I wouldn’t completely change that statement, as long as you keep upping the difficulty the more you play (particularly with the MORE EVENTS, MORE INSANITIES, and FRANTIC REAL-TIME settings), gameplay can also become pretty fun and interesting. There’s also a good bit of humor dashed around here in there, usually based off of the custodian’s various insanities, which is always fun to see. It will never get old to see progress bars like “Fixing myself…” and dialogue like “SO MUCH CLEANER” dashed around the most ludicrous ♥♥♥♥ ever lol. And although it doesn’t mesh the best with the more fun parts of Endless Dark’s gameplay, I have to say the atmosphere is certainly pretty great when it really is just you on that ship hurtling through space, truly no one there but yourself. I really do just love this game, and though I don’t know if it would be for everyone due to its particular blend of gameplay, if you like thought-provoking material based around a really interesting and great story, feel free to give this game a try. If I were to give any advice for if you were to start playing, only play as Robbie for the main story, play the campaigns in order, and keep cranking up the difficulty as you progress. I don't even know if what I've written here even covers everything I want to say because there really is just so much I liked about this game. I guess I'll just say that the story was really, really good, I especially loved the Turing Complete campaign, and thank you to the devs! You really managed to make something super special, even with as little resources as you had. Honestly what an excellent game.

I figured this would be a wild ride just based on the trailers, but nothing could have prepared me for the actual secrets this game was hiding, or the emotional rollercoaster that it would take me on. The minute-to-minute gameplay is mostly just reading and picking options from menus, and yet this still managed to be one of the most stressful games I've ever tried out. A+, I wish I could rip out my memory core and experience it for the first time again.

How this absolutely phenomenal game hasn't gotten more traction, I have no idea. Well, I have some idea. The game is difficult, and it can feel very unfair sometimes. But trust me when I say it's worth it. The writing in this game is phenomenal, and while you certainly can play the game on an easier difficulty to experience it, I think the difficulty adds weight to the story and helps you empathize with the main characters all the more as you move through it. Furthermore, the sound design of this game is another potentially controversial choice, but is masterfully done. You are subjected to near constant creaks, clangs, and rattles, and as your character's psychosis increase; audio glitches and distorted speaking. Fortunately, there is an option to turn them off if you find them truly unbearable. However, again I have to recommend you don't. It adds a layer of immersion, and every so often they line up with the absolutely wonderful music in this game to make it as beautiful as any symphony I've ever heard.
